paragraphs: A neural network can become less able to learn as training continues, making it harder to adapt to new tasks or changing data. This loss of plasticity motivates the paper. Although some familiar regularization methods help, the authors identify ordinary Dropout as ineffective for this particular problem.

The proposed method, Activation by Interval-wise Dropout, or AID, changes how units are dropped. It assigns different dropout probabilities to different intervals of preactivation values—the values computed before applying an activation function. This makes the subnetworks used during training depend on those intervals. The theoretical analysis connects this regularization to behavior resembling deep linear networks, which the abstract describes as avoiding plasticity loss.

Experiments support AID’s ability to preserve adaptability in continual image classification, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet. The authors also report improved reinforcement learning performance in the Arcade Learning Environment. Together, these results suggest that the placement and probability of dropout matter for continued learning: a targeted version can help where the standard method does not.
icml-2025-activation-by-interval-wise-dr.tldr: AID varies dropout probabilities across preactivation intervals to help neural networks retain their ability to learn.

paragraphs: Testing language models for jailbreak vulnerabilities often requires searching through many adversarial prompts. Human testing takes time, while automatically generated attacks can be difficult to read and hard to scale. This paper introduces AdvPrompter, a language model trained to produce readable adversarial prompts within seconds.

AdvPrompter learns through an alternating optimization procedure. Its outputs are suffixes appended to an input instruction, designed to disguise that instruction without changing its meaning and encourage the target model to produce a harmful response. The central contribution is a trained generator of adversarial text, making repeated prompt production a capability of the model itself.

The authors report highly competitive results on AdvBench and HarmBench against popular open-source target models, with attacks also transferring to closed-source models accessed as black boxes. They further find that training target models on AdvPrompter-generated suffixes is a promising way to improve jailbreak robustness. That defensive result is presented as a promising strategy, rather than a guarantee that adversarial training removes the vulnerability.
icml-2025-advprompter-fast-adaptive-adve.tldr: AdvPrompter learns to generate readable jailbreak prompts quickly and provides adversarial examples that may improve model robustness.

paragraphs: Safety testing needs to account for conversations in which a user adjusts their approach after each model response. The authors argue that many automated red-teaming methods do not capture this interaction well, while manual conversations are costly. GOAT automates this conversational form of adversarial testing using plain language.

The system uses a general-purpose model equipped with seven red-teaming attacks. It is prompted to reason about the available techniques, the target’s current response, and what to try next. This creates an adaptive testing agent whose choices depend on how the conversation unfolds. Its extensible design aims to automate repeated testing of known risks while allowing human testers to investigate new ones.

On JailbreakBench, the authors report ASR@10 results of 96% for Llama 3.1 8B, 91% for Llama 3.1 70B, and 94% for GPT-4o. These findings demonstrate GOAT’s effectiveness at identifying vulnerabilities in the evaluated models. The reported figures describe this benchmark evaluation; the broader contribution is a framework for scaling conversational stress tests.
icml-2025-automated-red-teaming-with-goa.tldr: GOAT automates adaptive, multi-turn adversarial conversations to uncover safety vulnerabilities in language models.

paragraphs: Individual neural activations are often difficult to explain in human terms. Sparse autoencoders transform them into a larger collection of latent features that can be more interpretable, but this can create millions of features to examine. The paper addresses that scale problem with an open-source pipeline that uses language models to generate and evaluate natural-language explanations.

The authors test the pipeline on sparse autoencoders with different sizes, activation functions, and training losses, built on two open-weight language models. They introduce five ways to score explanations that cost less to run than the previous state of the art. This makes evaluating interpretations part of the automated workflow, alongside producing them.

One method, intervention scoring, examines whether an explanation captures the effects of intervening on a latent feature. The authors find that this reveals interpretable latents missed by existing methods. They also offer guidance for explanations that hold across a broader range of activating contexts and identify pitfalls in scoring. The contribution therefore concerns both scalable explanation and how to assess its reliability.
icml-2025-automatically-interpreting-mil.tldr: An automated pipeline generates and evaluates explanations for sparse-autoencoder features, including through the effects of interventions.

paragraphs: Tree canopy height helps describe forest structure and supports estimates of above-ground biomass and assessments of ecological disruption. A map covering several years also makes it possible to examine forests over time. This paper develops a method for producing large-scale canopy height maps with both spatial detail and temporal coverage.

The model takes time series of Sentinel 2 satellite observations and predicts canopy height across multiple years. It learns from GEDI LiDAR measurements used as ground-truth height data. The resulting European map covers 2019–2022 at 10-metre resolution, which the authors describe as the first temporal canopy height product of this kind for the continent.

The authors also provide a detailed map for 2020 and report more precise height estimates than previous studies. Both the processing pipeline and temporal maps are publicly available. Their contribution combines a prediction method with a usable monitoring resource: researchers can study canopy height across a large geographic area and multiple years, supporting further forest and ecological analyses.
icml-2025-capturing-temporal-dynamics-in.tldr: A model trained with LiDAR measurements turns satellite time series into 10-metre canopy height maps of Europe across 2019–2022.

paragraphs: Equivariant neural networks encode how outputs should change when inputs undergo a symmetry transformation. Existing group-based approaches work with classical geometric spaces. This paper considers data described by non-commutative geometry, where the algebraic structure differs from that underlying ordinary compact matrix groups, making those existing approaches unsuitable for the stated setting.

The authors establish the existence of neural networks that respect symmetries described by compact matrix quantum groups. These structures extend the symmetry framework beyond the classical setting. The contribution is mathematical: it identifies a type of equivariant network appropriate to the non-commutative setting and studies the restrictions symmetry places on its weights.

For the class called easy compact matrix quantum groups, which are defined through set partitions, the paper characterizes the permitted weight matrices. This analysis also produces new descriptions of equivariant weights for some classical compact matrix groups. The work therefore expands the theoretical scope of symmetry-aware networks while yielding results relevant to familiar geometric settings as well.
icml-2025-compact-matrix-quantum-group-e.tldr: The paper establishes equivariant networks for compact matrix quantum-group symmetries and characterizes weights for an important subclass.

paragraphs: An ensemble combines multiple neural networks and can improve performance, but running all its members is computationally expensive. That cost becomes especially relevant for large models or settings with limited resources. Ensemble distillation addresses the problem by training a smaller student model to absorb knowledge from the collection of teacher models.

This paper focuses on transferring the ensemble’s diversity through distribution distillation. Its proposed method uses flow matching to carry that diversity into the student. The approach treats the ensemble as a source of varied predictive behavior to preserve, making the distribution of teacher outputs central to what the student learns.

The authors report extensive experiments demonstrating the method’s effectiveness relative to existing ensemble distillation approaches. The intended balance is a student that is inexpensive to use while retaining performance comparable to its teacher ensemble. The stated findings support the proposed transfer method, with the main significance being a way to make ensemble knowledge more practical when the full collection of networks is costly to deploy.
icml-2025-ensemble-distribution-distilla.tldr: Flow matching helps distill an ensemble’s predictive diversity into a smaller student model.

paragraphs: Language models are often expected to produce text with exact structural rules, such as formatted data or code. Grammar-constrained decoding enforces a specified context-free grammar by blocking tokens that would lead outside it. The challenge is to make these decisions efficiently while preserving the guarantee that the generated structure follows the grammar.

A key difficulty is that the model’s subword tokens do not necessarily match the units used by the grammar. The decoding algorithm must work out how those two systems align and use that information to construct token masks. Existing approaches can spend tens of minutes preprocessing common grammars before generation begins.

The paper introduces an algorithm and implementation that make offline preprocessing 17.71 times faster than existing approaches while retaining state-of-the-art efficiency for mask computation during generation. The improvement targets the preparation stage without sacrificing the stated online efficiency. This matters because grammar enforcement involves both an initial setup cost and repeated decisions as the model generates its structured output.
icml-2025-flexible-and-efficient-grammar.tldr: A grammar-constrained decoding algorithm speeds preprocessing by 17.71 times while maintaining state-of-the-art online masking efficiency.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns how to act from an existing dataset. Flow Q-learning uses a flow-matching policy to represent the potentially complex distribution of actions in that data. Such expressive modeling is attractive, but flow policies generate actions iteratively, which complicates training them to favor actions with higher estimated value.

FQL handles this by training an expressive one-step policy with reinforcement learning instead of directly optimizing the iterative flow policy for value. The authors state that this avoids unstable recursive backpropagation and removes the need for iterative action generation at test time. The resulting policy still retains most of the expressivity, making the generation procedure simpler without fully giving up the modeling benefit.

Experiments cover 73 state-based and pixel-based tasks from OGBench and D4RL. The authors report strong performance both when learning offline and when moving from offline learning to online interaction. The findings support the central design choice: a one-step policy can make expressive action modeling practical for value-driven learning and action selection.
icml-2025-flow-q-learning-273b950732.tldr: Flow Q-learning combines expressive flow-based action modeling with a one-step policy to simplify reinforcement learning and inference.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can struggle with multi-step visual reasoning even when language models handle equivalent text problems more successfully. The paper studies this modality imbalance in a controlled synthetic framework. It includes Table Readout, Grid Navigation, and Visual Analogy, each with SIMPLE and HARD versions and corresponding text-only tasks.

Even the SIMPLE visual tasks challenge frontier models. The authors investigate training strategies that use these easier tasks to improve performance on the harder versions. Matching visual and text formulations lets them measure how much difficulty comes from the presentation modality and how different training approaches change that gap.

The study finds that explicit image-to-text conversion helps transfer reasoning from text and supports generalization from simple to hard visual problems. It also shows that this conversion can be internalized at test time. Mechanistic analysis identifies gradient-alignment measures that help identify promising training strategies, while ablations highlight chain-of-thought’s importance. These findings connect improved generalization to both the training procedure and how visual information becomes available for reasoning.
icml-2025-generalizing-from-simple-to-ha.tldr: Controlled visual reasoning tasks show how image-to-text conversion can help models generalize from simple training problems to harder ones.

paragraphs: Generating speech directly over several minutes creates unusually long token sequences. The authors identify coherence loss, difficulties with long-sequence training or extrapolation, and inference memory costs as obstacles for textless spoken language models. These problems motivate SpeechSSM, a model family designed for sustained speech generation without an intermediate text representation.

SpeechSSM uses advances in linear-time sequence modeling to learn from and generate long spoken audio in a single decoding session. The abstract gives 16-minute read or extemporaneous speech as an example. The authors report substantially better coherence and efficiency than current Transformer spoken language models on multi-minute outputs, while matching their performance at the utterance level.

The paper also addresses evaluation, finding existing speech-language assessments uninformative for this longer setting. It introduces LibriSpeech-Long, embedding-based and language-model-judged metrics, and measurements of quality over length and time. These additions matter because success at generating a short utterance does not adequately describe how a model performs throughout an extended spoken passage.
icml-2025-long-form-speech-generation-wi.tldr: SpeechSSM generates multi-minute speech without text intermediates and introduces evaluation tools for sustained audio generation.

paragraphs: Networks with continuous piecewise-linear activations represent functions through regions where their behavior is linear. This paper introduces local complexity to measure how densely those regions occur over an input data distribution. The distribution matters: the measure describes complexity in relation to the inputs being considered, rather than treating all parts of input space equally.

The authors prove that ReLU networks learning low-dimensional feature representations have lower local complexity. This connects properties of learned weight matrices to the geometry of the functions those networks implement. It provides a theoretical link between learning a compact representation and producing a function with less local regional complexity.

The paper further shows that local complexity upper-bounds the function’s total variation over the input distribution, establishing a route for relating feature learning to adversarial robustness. It also considers how optimization pushes networks toward lower-complexity solutions. The contribution is a framework connecting representation learning, functional variation, and network geometry, with robustness appearing through the stated theoretical relationship.
icml-2025-on-the-local-complexity-of-lin.tldr: A measure of local linear-region density links low-dimensional ReLU representations to functional variation and adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: Engineering optimization often requires reducing a cost while satisfying strict constraints. Learned proxies aim to approximate these decisions, but the authors identify limited labeled data and short training budgets as difficult conditions for standard deep neural networks. They propose a semi-supervised Bayesian neural network designed for this constrained setting.

Training alternates between two complementary steps. A supervised step learns to minimize cost, and an unsupervised step works on constraint feasibility. This alternating arrangement gives both the objective and the constraints an explicit role in training. The Bayesian model also provides posterior samples, which the authors use to construct probabilistic confidence bounds on performance from limited validation data.

On important non-convex problems in energy network operations, the proposed model outperforms the evaluated deep neural network architectures. Reported gains include up to a tenfold reduction in the expected maximum equality gap and a halving of inequality gaps. These findings concern how closely proposed solutions satisfy constraints, while the confidence bounds provide an additional way to assess expected performance under scarce validation data.
icml-2025-optimization-proxies-using-lim.tldr: A semi-supervised Bayesian optimization proxy improves constraint satisfaction under limited data and training time while providing probabilistic performance bounds.

paragraphs: Symmetric tensors appear in statistics, machine learning, graph theory, and several scientific fields. Learning from them raises a structural question: how should a network respond when the underlying coordinates are permuted? Permutation equivariance requires the output to transform consistently with that reordering, allowing the model to respect the relevant symmetry.

The paper gives two different characterizations of all linear permutation-equivariant functions between symmetric power spaces of real coordinate vectors. This supplies a complete description of the linear maps satisfying the chosen symmetry in that setting. It addresses a gap in earlier work, which had not explored symmetric tensors as inputs to permutation-equivariant models and had largely emphasized Euclidean symmetries.

On two tasks, the authors find that the resulting functions are highly data efficient compared with standard multilayer perceptrons. They also report potential for generalization to symmetric tensors of different sizes. The empirical findings support the usefulness of encoding this structure, while the cross-size result remains framed as potential rather than an established guarantee.
icml-2025-permutation-equivariant-neural.tldr: Two complete characterizations of permutation-equivariant linear maps enable data-efficient learning from symmetric tensors.

paragraphs: A sequence model’s allocated memory does not directly describe how it uses past information to generate future outputs. This paper introduces effective state-size, or ESS, as a quantitative measure of memory utilization. The goal is to provide more interpretable and actionable information than cache size or visual inspections of operators such as attention maps.

Drawing on signal processing and control theory, ESS applies to systems with input-invariant or input-varying linear operators. This scope includes variants of attention, convolution, and recurrence, enabling analysis across different kinds of sequence-processing components. The shared framework focuses on internal mechanisms for retaining and using information from earlier inputs.

The authors show applications to initialization, regularization, and distillation aimed at improving the performance-efficiency tradeoff. They also examine how context delimiters, including end-of-speech tokens, affect ESS and reveal differences in memory use across language-model architectures. The contribution is both a measurement framework and evidence that its measurements can guide choices about how sequence models are trained and made more efficient.
icml-2025-quantifying-memory-utilization.tldr: Effective state-size measures how sequence models use memory and helps guide training, regularization, and distillation.

paragraphs: A generator may produce valid outputs while representing some groups disproportionately. This paper extends a theoretical framework for generation to incorporate proportional representation of groups from the training data. Its definition makes representativeness an explicit requirement, bringing diversity and bias concerns into the mathematical description of successful generation.

The authors characterize representative generation in both uniform and non-uniform settings. They introduce group closure dimension as a key combinatorial quantity for this analysis. They also study generation in the limit, considering both whether representative generation is possible in principle and whether it can be achieved computationally.

For countably infinite hypothesis classes and collections of groups, the paper establishes feasibility under certain conditions. It also proves a negative computability result when only membership queries are available. That result contrasts with positive results for standard generation in the same broader theoretical tradition. The distinction matters because adding proportional representation changes what can be achieved with a given form of information access, even when ordinary generation is possible.
icml-2025-representative-language-genera.tldr: A theoretical framework defines proportionally representative generation and establishes conditional feasibility alongside computational limits.

paragraphs: Embodied agents can benefit from larger models, more data, and more computation. This paper asks how those benefits scale when agents are pretrained on offline datasets. It considers imitation learning, which models an agent’s behavior, and world modeling, which models its environment, both using generative learning objectives.

The authors find power-law relationships of the same broad types observed in language modeling, including relationships involving loss and optimal model size. This turns a general expectation of improvement with scale into a more quantitative description. Such relationships are relevant to deciding how to allocate resources between model capacity and training data.

The coefficients of these laws depend strongly on the tokenizer, task, and architecture. Consequently, the shared mathematical form does not imply that every setting should use the same model or dataset size. The paper’s main finding combines regularity with dependence on design choices: scaling patterns carry over to these agent-learning tasks, but their practical implications must account for the particular representation and system being trained.
icml-2025-scaling-laws-for-pre-training-.tldr: Agent pretraining exhibits power-law scaling, but tokenizer, task, and architecture strongly affect optimal model and data sizes.

paragraphs: Scientific data often varies across both space and time, arrives at irregular locations, and contains large volumes of measurements. Missing sensor readings and detailed simulations make those challenges especially relevant. SCENT is designed to learn continuous spatiotemporal representations while handling the computational demands of such data.

The framework brings interpolation, reconstruction, and forecasting into one transformer-based encoder-processor-decoder architecture. Learnable queries support generalization, and query-wise cross-attention captures dependencies at multiple scales. A sparse attention mechanism helps the system scale with data size and model complexity, while supporting flexible outputs and efficient evaluation at arbitrary resolutions.

The authors evaluate SCENT using simulations and real-world experiments, reporting state-of-the-art performance across multiple challenging tasks alongside superior scalability. The significance is the combination of capabilities within a single architecture: estimating values between observations, reconstructing data, and predicting future behavior all use the same framework. Its resolution flexibility also connects the learned representation to the locations and detail level needed for a particular output.
icml-2025-scent-robust-spatiotemporal-le.tldr: SCENT unifies scientific interpolation, reconstruction, and forecasting with scalable attention and outputs at arbitrary resolutions.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can describe objects that are not actually supported by an image. SECOND addresses this perceptual hallucination problem by changing how visual information is selected and contrasted during decoding. Its central idea is to use information from multiple scales in a way organized around objects.

The method progressively selects and integrates visual evidence at different scales. It then repeatedly contrasts that information to support a more precise interpretation of the image. This makes both prioritization and comparison part of the process: the system does not simply rely on the presence of multiple scales, but actively determines how their information contributes.

The authors report significant reductions in perceptual hallucination and improvements over existing methods across a wide range of benchmarks. Their theoretical analysis and experiments point to multi-scale processing as an underexplored source of improvement for vision-language models. The findings support the specific strategy of selecting and contrasting across scales as a way to make generated descriptions more closely grounded in visual evidence.
icml-2025-second-mitigating-perceptual-h.tldr: SECOND reduces visual hallucinations by progressively selecting and contrasting object-centered information across image scales.

paragraphs: Multi-speaker transcription needs to determine both what was said and who said it. Speaker labels introduce a permutation problem because assigning identities consistently is part of the learning task. Sortformer is an encoder-based diarization model designed to supply speaker supervision to speech-to-text systems while addressing this ambiguity.

The paper introduces Sort Loss, which uses sorted objectives and can operate alone or together with permutation-invariant loss. It also proposes a multi-speaker transcription architecture that embeds speaker labels into the encoder through sinusoidal kernel functions. This connects speaker information expressed through timestamps with the tokens in the output transcription.

Experiments show that Sort Loss can improve diarization and that Sortformer’s supervision improves multi-speaker transcription accuracy. The authors anticipate that this design will help integrate speaker tagging into foundational speech-to-text systems and multimodal language models. That wider integration is presented as an expected application, while the reported experimental findings concern diarization and transcription. Code and trained models are available through NVIDIA NeMo.
icml-2025-sortformer-a-novel-approach-fo.tldr: Sortformer uses sorted speaker objectives to improve diarization and provide effective speaker supervision for multi-speaker transcription.

paragraphs: Offline policy evaluation estimates the future discounted return of a fixed policy using an existing dataset. Its learning procedure can become unstable or diverge when state-action representations are poorly suited to the task. This paper investigates whether bisimulation-based representation learning can improve stability, meaning convergence to the value-learning procedure’s fixed point.

The proposed algorithm, kernel representations for offline policy evaluation, or krope, uses a kernel to shape those representations. State-action pairs should be represented similarly when they have similar immediate rewards and lead to similar next state-action pairs under the target policy. This ties representational similarity to the behavior relevant for evaluating that particular policy.

The authors show that krope learns stable representations and produces lower value error than the evaluated baselines. Their analysis supplies theoretical insight into why bisimulation-based methods can stabilize value learning. The result matters because it treats representation design as a direct part of making offline evaluation reliable, linking the structure of learned features to both convergence and estimation accuracy.
icml-2025-stable-offline-value-function-.tldr: Krope shapes state-action representations using reward and transition similarity to improve the stability and accuracy of offline policy evaluation.

paragraphs: A language model’s internal representations are trained for coherent language, so truthful and hallucinated content may not separate clearly within them. This paper proposes the Truthfulness Separator Vector, or TSV, to make that distinction easier to detect. The vector steers representations during inference without changing the language model’s parameters.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, a small labeled set teaches TSV to form compact, separated clusters for truthful and hallucinated content. The method then expands the exemplars using unlabeled model generations. An optimal-transport algorithm assigns provisional labels, and a confidence filter selects examples for this augmentation process.

The authors report state-of-the-art detection performance with little labeled data and strong generalization across datasets. The contribution is a lightweight way to reshape the information used by a hallucination detector while leaving the underlying model parameters intact. The findings support improved separation and detection of hallucinated content; the method’s stated role is to identify that content through steered representations.
icml-2025-steer-llm-latents-for-hallucin.tldr: TSV steers language-model representations to improve hallucination detection using a small labeled set and filtered pseudo-labels.

paragraphs: Functional ANOVA explains a high-dimensional function as a sum of lower-dimensional components. These components can make a model easier to interpret, but a single function may admit multiple decompositions. As a result, neural networks can produce unstable component estimates even when they are modeling the same overall relationship.

ANOVA Tensor Product Neural Network, or ANOVA-TPNN, addresses this ambiguity through an architecture that guarantees a unique functional ANOVA decomposition. Its design is motivated by tensor-product basis expansions. The authors also prove that the network can approximate any smooth function well, connecting the interpretability structure to a broad approximation capability.

Empirically, the method gives much more stable component estimates than existing neural networks when training data and initial parameter values change. This matters because an explanation based on individual components is easier to rely on when it remains consistent across those variations. The paper combines a uniqueness guarantee for the decomposition with experimental evidence that the resulting interpretations are more stable in practice.
icml-2025-tensor-product-neural-networks.tldr: ANOVA-TPNN guarantees a unique functional decomposition and produces more stable component-based interpretations.

paragraphs: Function calling lets a language model respond to a request by invoking an external tool, API, or user-defined function. Evaluating this ability requires deciding whether calls are valid and collecting diverse functions that reflect real use. BFCL provides a benchmark designed to address both challenges across a broad range of settings.

Its tasks include serial and parallel calls in multiple programming languages, using functions and prompts supplied by experts and users. A new evaluation method based on abstract syntax trees supports scaling to thousands of functions. The benchmark also tests whether models refrain from calling tools when appropriate and reason through multi-step tasks that involve state.

Across the evaluated models, the authors find that leading systems perform well on single-turn function calls, while memory, dynamic decisions, and long-horizon reasoning remain difficult. This gives the benchmark a role beyond measuring isolated tool invocation: it distinguishes that capability from managing an extended agentic task. The results identify continuing challenges in coordinating tool use over time.
icml-2025-the-berkeley-function-calling-.tldr: BFCL evaluates tool calling from individual invocations to stateful tasks, revealing persistent challenges in memory and long-horizon reasoning.

paragraphs: Detecting an abnormal event as it happens differs from predicting the specific future time when it will occur. This paper focuses on that latter task, called anomaly prediction. The authors argue that existing time-series methods either concentrate on immediate anomalies or do not give sufficiently precise predictions of future abnormal points.

Their framework, Anomaly to Prompt, combines Anomaly-Aware Forecasting with Synthetic Anomaly Prompting. The forecasting component learns relationships involving anomalies so that it can predict abnormal time points. The prompting component uses a learnable Anomaly Prompt Pool to simulate diverse abnormal patterns through prompts adapted to the signal, supporting robust anomaly detection.

Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show better performance than state-of-the-art methods and support the framework’s ability to forecast future anomalies. The contribution brings anomaly relationships directly into forecasting and uses synthetic patterns to broaden the anomaly behavior represented by the model. Its practical focus is timing: predicting upcoming abnormal points gives the task a more specific target than recognizing that a signal is already unusual.
icml-2025-when-will-it-fail-anomaly-to-p.tldr: A2P combines anomaly-aware forecasting and synthetic anomaly prompts to predict when future abnormal events will occur.
